title: Update on the Aryan Invasion Debate
byline: by Koenraad Elst · Aditya Prakashan · 1999 · conference papers from Atlanta and Madison (1996), revised
lede: Did Indo-European speech come into India with migrants from the steppes around 1500 BC, or did it spread out from India? Elst sets out the case against the Aryan Invasion Theory (AIT), drawing on Vedic astronomy, linguistics, archaeology, the horse, physical anthropology, and a long review of the French scholar Bernard Sergent's defence of it. He does not claim his side has won, and calls on both camps to keep doubting. He also covers the politics: how the theory came to be used against Hindus, and how its critics get labelled Nazis.

note: Elst argues a minority position. Most linguists and geneticists today support a migration of Indo-European speakers into India in the 2nd millennium BC, though not a violent “invasion”. This page sets out his arguments as his own and does not decide the question.

sections.title: How a linguistic theory became politics
sections.lede: Elst's first claim is that the AIT carries more political weight than any other question of ancient history.
items: Race theories borrow the word “Aryan”. Elst notes that Hitler, if anything, favoured the AIT.
Brahmins as foreign conquerors, an early Indian political use of the theory.
The Justice Party, later the Dravida Kazhagam.
From The Menace of Hindu Imperialism to Dalit Voice, which calls Brahmins “the Jews of India”.
Elst says Marxist historians such as Romila Thapar and R.S. Sharma label the theory's critics Nazis instead of answering them.

sections.title: Dates written in the sky
sections.lede: Elst's strongest evidence for an early date is astronomy. Some Vedic texts describe star positions that, because of the slow precession of the equinoxes, only held in particular eras.
items: The Scottish mathematician argues that Hindu astronomical tables record real ancient observations, not later calculations back in time.
Tradition records a conjunction of the seven planets near the star Revati on this date.
The Pleiades “never swerve from the East”
Read as the spring equinox in the Pleiades, which fixes an early date.
Includes the theorem usually credited to Pythagoras, along with a stellar marker (Regulus at the summer solstice).
An afternoon, non-total solar eclipse on the Kurukshetra meridian. Its conditions limit the possible dates.
Possibly the Zodiac, which is usually dated to Babylon c. 600 BC.
sections.after: His conclusion from this chapter: the Rigveda was completed by the 4th millennium BC, too early for an invasion in the 2nd.

sections.title: Elst's scorecard
head: Evidence
Usually read as
Elst's reading
rows: Linguistics
Homeland on the steppes, with Sanskrit far from Proto-Indo-European
Inconclusive. Arguments from plants and animals fail, and the language contacts point both ways.
The horse
Brought in by the invaders
Horse remains at Harappan sites, Mohenjo-daro by 2500 BC at the latest. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
Mitanni (15th c. BC)
Aryans on their way to India
Kings in Mesopotamia with Vedic gods and Indic words, and no trace of a journey east.
Vedic texts
Memories of a foreign homeland
No Urheimat (original homeland) is remembered. The Puranas instead record emigrations out of India.
“Dasa”, “black”, “Asura”
Dark-skinned natives defeated by fair invaders
Following Ambedkar: these are moral or ritual terms, not racial ones.
Physical anthropology
Newcomers from Central Asia c. 1500 BC
Hemphill and Christensen find no such influx. Kenoyer finds the indigenous population was not displaced.
Archaeology (Sergent)
Bactria and Pirak as stages of the invasion
Ambiguous. Bactria reads as Iranian, and Harappa's decline needs no invaders.

sections.title: Not a closed case
items: “Let us keep on doubting.” Elst says neither invasion nor indigenous origin is proven.
He admits no linguistic argument yet decides for an Indian homeland.
He criticises Indian authors who exaggerate, for example “Greater India” theories, or Rama in the Avesta.
